newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Aboriginal babies seen twice as likely to be stillborn.
newsitem.headline: Aboriginal babies seen twice as likely to be stillborn.

text.p: Aboriginal babies are twice as likely to be stillborn than non-indigenous Australian infants and their death rate in the first four weeks of life is two to six times higher, according to a study released on Wednesday.

The study of indigenous mothers and babies, using the latest data available from between 1991 and 1993, found poverty within Australia's aboriginal communities was a major contributor to the higher death rates.

"Indigenous babies suffer (stillborn) death rates twice that of other babies in Australia and low birthweight is a major factor," said Dr Paul Lancaster, author of the study by the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare at Sydney University.
The low birthweight was caused by poor nutrition during pregnancy and a high rate of diabetes and cigarette smoking in the aboriginal community, he said.
The national stillborn rate among aboriginal babies was 15.9 per 1,000 births, compared with 6.7 in the wider population, Lancaster told Reuters.

There are no national figures for the neonatal death rate, which records the number of babies who die in the first four weeks. But figures in Australian states with large aboriginal populations revealed a neonatal death rate two to six times greater than for non-indigenous babies.

In the Northern Territory, the Aboriginal death rate was 14.6 per 1,000 births compared with 6.4 for non-indigenous babies, in South Australia it was 19 compared with 3.3, in Western Australia it was 8.3 against 3.3 and in Queensland it was 10.3 to 4.4.
Lancaster, director of the institute's national perinatal statistics unit, said the higher death rates among aboriginal babies was a result of lower community health standards.
Aboriginal adults have a life expectancy 10 to 15 years lower than the rest of the population. Aborigines make up some 300,000 of the country's 18 million population.
The study also found that health education was deficient because aboriginal women began giving birth at younger ages, with a high rate of births by poorly educated teenagers.
